extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, appellate attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Appellate guidance from the Federal Circuit on standards and legal tests applied in patent litigation (inequitable conduct, unclean hands, obviousness, summary judgment, attorney-fee and costs determinations). Focused on how courts evaluate facts, intent, materiality, and procedural issues on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclean hands doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may find unclean hands when the misconduct of a party seeking relief 'has immediate and necessary relation to the equity that he seeks in respect of the matter in litigation' and involves 'violations of conscience as in some measure affect the equitable relations between the parties' (Keystone Driller Co. v. Gen. Excavator Co.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the 'immediate and necessary' nexus between the misconduct and the relief sought; consider totality of misconduct (not necessarily limited to the district court's enumerated bases); examples of misconduct supporting unclean hands include failing to disclose related patent applications during discovery, attempting to block discovery of prior art searches, evasive or false testimony, and deceit in litigation. A court may affirm on any adequately supported ground in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for unclean hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of a district court's ruling of unclean hands is for abuse of discretion; factual findings supporting the ruling are reviewed only for clear error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts consider the totality of evidence-supported misconduct and will affirm absent clear error in the district court's factual findings or abuse of discretion in the equitable determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct test (Therasense)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove inequitable conduct, a party must show that the patentee withheld material information from the PTO and did so with the specific intent to deceive the PTO (Therasense). Both materiality and deceptive intent must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deceptive intent must be 'the single most reasonable inference' from the evidence. Both prongs are required; evaluate them separately and together when deciding unenforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality — but-for standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An undisclosed prior art reference is but-for material 'if the PTO would not have allowed a claim had it been aware of' the reference (Therasense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On remand courts must evaluate whether the PTO's patentability decision may have differed if the undisclosed material had been accurately and fully presented. Even references disclosed to the PTO may be but-for material if the patentee mischaracterized them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per se materiality for affirmative egregious misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of 'affirmative egregious misconduct,' materiality may be established per se without needing a but-for showing (Therasense/Aventis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should determine whether misrepresentations rise to 'affirmative egregious misconduct' such that per se materiality applies, and make express findings on this separate issue rather than folding it into intent analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative-reference principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference that is merely cumulative of what the examiner already had is not but-for material (Cal. Inst. of Tech. v. Broadcom; Regeneron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is cumulative when it teaches no more than what a reasonable examiner would consider taught by the prior art already before the PTO. If undisclosed references might teach more than the mischaracterized/disclosed reference, they may be material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate evaluation of deceptive intent
rubrics_metrics.description: A court must consider multiple acts of misconduct 'in the aggregate' when inferring deceptive intent; individual acts that are innocent or explainable in isolation may, taken together, demonstrate intent to deceive (Nilssen; Ohio Willow; Apotex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On remand or review, courts should reassess intent based on the collective weight of all misrepresentations, omissions, misleading filings, and conduct during prosecution and related prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for inequitable conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Both materiality and deceptive intent must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts review the district court's factual findings on these elements for clear error and the ultimate equitable determination for abuse of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mischaracterized but-disclosed references still potentially material
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a prior art reference was disclosed to the PTO, it may still be but-for material where the patentee mischaracterized it (TransWeb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the patentee's representations about a disclosed reference materially affected the examiner's evaluation such that the outcome might have differed if represented accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: False or evasive testimony as misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentional testimonial falsehoods and evasive testimony can constitute misconduct supporting unclean hands or inequitable conduct (see Gilead and related discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether false testimony deprived the adversary or the court of material information, and whether it forms part of a pattern showing intent or unconscionable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment — genuine dispute of material fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary judgment is improper where genuine disputes of material fact exist; issues such as whether prior art discloses claim elements, embodiment equivalence, or functionality are fact questions that must go to the trier of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On summary judgment courts must draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party. 'Common sense' or similar extrapolations used to support obviousness at summary judgment must be articulated with sufficient clarity for review (Perfect Web; Plantronics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — motivation to combine and factual nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine prior art disclosures is a question of fact (University of Strathclyde v. Clear-Vu).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts must not resolve genuinely disputed factual issues (e.g., whether prior art teaches essential claim elements or whether a marketed product embodies prior art) on summary judgment; motivation to combine requires articulated reasoning if relying on 'common sense.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia — such as copying by competitors and commercial success — are relevant to nonobviousness and must be considered by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must evaluate evidence of objective indicia and the required nexus to the claimed features in the light most favorable to the non-moving party; genuine disputes on these facts preclude summary judgment of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on evidence like commercial success or copying as objective indicia, a nexus is required between those indicia and the patented features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record must support a reasonable factfinder's conclusion that the success or copying is attributable to the claimed features, not to extraneous factors; disputed nexus issues require factfinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction and prosecution history relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history of related applications and examiner statements (e.g., indefiniteness re planar vs cambered) can materially bear on claim construction and litigation strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding related prosecution history can undermine an adversary's ability to frame claim construction and defenses; failure to disclose such materials may support unclean hands or inequitable conduct findings if relevant and withheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of inequitable conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequitable conduct, if proven, renders a patent unenforceable and is an affirmative defense to infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must separately evaluate materiality and intent, applying clear-and-convincing evidence standards for facts and abuse-of-discretion review for the equitable determination of unenforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 285 exceptional-case framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 285 allows awarding reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party in 'exceptional' cases; the inquiry is two-step: (1) determine whether the case is 'exceptional' and (2) if so, exercise discretion whether to award fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'exceptional' case is one that stands out in the substantive strength of a party's litigating position or the unreasonable manner of litigation (Octane Fitness). Consider totality of circumstances; district courts must assess circumstances and appellate review is for abuse of discretion (fee prevailing-party determination is de novo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevailing party determination under § 285
rubrics_metrics.description: A prevailing party is one that effects a material alteration in the legal relationship between the parties (Shum; B.E. Tech.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dismissal with prejudice of an opponent's counterclaims (resulting in inability to enforce patents against accused products) constitutes a material alteration qualifying the movant as the prevailing party; a party need not prevail on all claims to be 'prevailing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs under Federal Rule 54(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Fifth Circuit law (applicable here), there is a strong presumption that the prevailing party will be awarded costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a district court denies or reduces costs, it must articulate justifications for doing so; the court may revisit cost awards after remanded proceedings resolve outstanding substantive issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional-circuit law and appellate review of summary judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant of summary judgment is reviewed according to the law of the regional circuit (here, Fifth Circuit); the Fifth Circuit reviews summary judgment de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate review looks to whether genuine disputes of material fact existed and whether the district court properly articulated factual and legal bases (especially when invoking 'common sense' in obviousness determinations).
